column2: Broad Street in front of the New York Stock Exchange in November 1968: the monumental stone columns and pediment, period parked sedans, police barriers, and a happening in progress: dancers in body paint covered head to toe in big painted polka dots, the columns, sedans, barriers and pavement spreading into a continuous field of red, white and black polka dots, placards reading COUNTED, bewildered brokers in grey suits, hard afternoon light, tactile limestone.

West 19th Street in Chelsea outside the industrial gallery buildings, looking toward the avenue: brickwork, loading doors, parked cars, plane trees, fire hydrants and pigeons all completely repainted red with white polka dots, giant yellow pumpkins with black dots on the sidewalk, a long queue of visitors doubling around dotted barriers holding tickets, wet pavement reflecting the dots, gallery signs reading NEW YORKERS, morning light.

A SoHo side street at night in 1979: cast iron facades, battered steel freight doors, wheat paste residue, broken streetlight, parked 1970s cars, a doorway tagged in black spray paint with a short cryptic poem signed with a copyright mark, scrawled crowns and arrows on the shutters, torn xerox flyers, steam from a manhole, a pedestrian in a long coat walking away, sodium light, documentary grit.

Great Jones Street in NoHo, looking along the block from a narrow brick building: every facade, steel shutter, parked car, curb and garbage bag repainted in the style of Jean-Michel Basquiat, black oilstick crowns, skeletal anatomical diagrams, scraped yellow and red fields, copyright marks, crossed out words reading COUNTED and N3W, wet asphalt, rust, morning light, pedestrians stopping to look.

A New York subway platform in 1982: sooty white tiles, riveted steel columns, greenish fluorescent light, empty advertising frames covered in matte black paper with fresh white chalk line drawings in the style of Keith Haring, radiant babies, barking dogs, dancing figures, a man in a denim jacket drawing with chalk, commuters watching, a transit cop approaching down the platform, a train arriving with headlights.

The handball wall beside the Harlem River Drive at East 128th Street on a bright summer day, the whole neighbourhood wrapped in the style of Keith Haring: orange walls with thick black outlined dancing figures, radiant babies and barking dogs covering the handball wall, chain link fence, highway barriers, brownstones, a bus and lampposts behind, kids playing handball, cyclists, a fire hydrant spraying, saturated colour.

A dim Japanese print gallery in a great Fifth Avenue museum: low warm light, pale wood floor, paper coloured walls, a long glass vitrine holding a famous woodblock print of a great blue wave, folding screens with painted waves, visitors leaning close to the glass with their hands behind their backs, doorways repeating into further galleries, soft glazing reflections, hushed and precise.

The Battery at the tip of Manhattan on the evening of October 29, 2012 during the storm surge, rendered as if Hokusai had carved it: a towering Prussian blue wave with white clawed foam curling over the harbour, the Statue of Liberty small in the distance like Mount Fuji, flooded paving and harbour railings, the round stone fort, rain lines, people in raincoats leaning into the wind, beige paper sky, woodblock outlines over a photoreal scene.

A small uptown gallery in a townhouse at 4 East 77th Street in February 1962: white painted walls, polished wood floor, a fireplace, modest doorways, cold Manhattan daylight from tall windows, large comic strip paintings with Ben-Day dots and thick black outlines hung on the walls, visitors in wool coats and hats, one holding a cigarette, a coat rack, genteel and astonished.

Times Square on a bright morning repainted overnight in the style of Roy Lichtenstein: every billboard, building, taxi, sidewalk and lamppost covered in Ben-Day dots, thick black outlines and flat primary red, yellow and blue, huge empty speech balloons over the crowd, a yellow explosion burst on a screen, comic speed lines, billboards reading NEW YORKERS and COUNTED, a crowd of tourists.

Fifth Avenue at 56th Street at night in March 1939, seen from inside a department store display window: a fur lined bathtub with a mannequin, theatrical spotlights, a bed of red coals, and the big plate glass window shattered outward with shards on the sidewalk, a policeman and astonished pedestrians in 1930s overcoats and hats outside, period taxis, wet street reflecting the light, stone facades.

The 1939 World's Fair at Flushing Meadows in the style of Salvador Dali: a surreal pavilion with a coral spiked facade and a giant Venus, the great white sphere and spire melting like soft wax over the fountains, a giant gold pocket watch draped over a lamppost with its hands at 4:20, elephants on impossibly long spindly legs walking in the distance, long shadows across a golden plaza, fairgoers in 1939 clothes, a still pond reflecting swans.

The Silver Factory loft at 231 East 47th Street in 1964: every wall, pipe and column wrapped in crumpled silver foil and silver paint, a battered red couch, a 16 mm movie camera on a tripod pointed at a stool, silkscreens of soup cans labelled N3W SOUP drying on the floor, floating silver pillow balloons, a hard flash, partygoers with sunglasses lounging, a payphone.

West 34th Street at night looking toward the Empire State Building, silkscreened in the style of Andy Warhol: the street printed as a grid of four repeating panels in hot pink, yellow, cyan and orange with misregistered black ink, yellow taxis, crowds, a 16 mm camera on a tripod in the street aimed at the tower, the tower floodlit, billboards reading N3W SOUP and COUNTED.

A crowded white museum gallery with pale wood floors and a luminous ceiling: a crowd of visitors all holding up phones toward a small famous painting of a swirling starry night over a village with a dark cypress, a velvet rope, a guard on a stool, other paintings on the side walls, the phone screens glowing, a child on a parent's shoulders.

Washington Street in DUMBO at night with the Manhattan Bridge framed between brick warehouses and the Brooklyn Bridge beyond, all painted in the style of Vincent van Gogh: a huge swirling starry sky of cobalt and chrome yellow impasto spirals, the Empire State Building rising like a dark flaming cypress, glowing yellow windows, cobblestones with painted reflections, couples walking, thick visible brushstrokes everywhere.

A modernist restaurant corridor of travertine, bronze and warm walnut inside a 1959 Park Avenue tower, a monumental painted theatre curtain from a 1919 Spanish ballet hanging the full height of the passage: two figures on a balcony above a bullring crowd in ochre, rose and cream, theatrical cloth texture, diners in tailored suits walking past, waiters, a chain metal curtain glinting, warm dinner light.

Rockefeller Plaza in winter repainted overnight in Picasso's cubist style: the tall tower, flags and sunken ice rink fractured into ochre, grey and bottle green planes with charcoal outlines, the golden statue over the rink broken into facets, a huge Christmas tree as stacked green triangles, skaters with faces shown from front and profile at once, snow, separated depth layers.

A plain pavement art stall beside the stone wall of Central Park on an October afternoon: a folding table with small black and white spray paint stencil canvases of rats, balloons and children, a hand written sign that says SPRAY ART $60, an elderly vendor dozing on a folding chair, joggers, dog walkers and tourists walking past without looking, autumn trees, a hot dog cart, horse carriage in the distance, warm light.

The Meatpacking District at blue hour, a grimy unbranded slaughterhouse delivery truck with slatted sides crammed with stuffed plush lambs, pigs, cows and chickens peering out, cobblestones, steel meat market canopies, loading docks, black and white spray paint street stencils of rats and a child with a red balloon on every wall and shutter, a few pedestrians filming with phones, wet cobblestones, street lamps.
